extracted.intended_audience: maritime historians, sailors, shipowners, and sailing-ship enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical standards for judging the performance, design, handling and operational practices of late-19th/early-20th century sailing ships (passage times, spar plans, crew training, cargo handling, seamanship in hazards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage time thresholds (under 80 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: PASSAGES TO SYDNEY UNDER 80 DAYS / PASSAGES TO MELBOURNE UNDER 80 DAYS — ships making passages under 80 days are singled out as notable performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists and tables of ships that made passages under 80 days (to Sydney and Melbourne) are used as a primary benchmark of success; examples and tabulated departures, equator crossing, Cape meridian, Otway/Leeuwin passed, arrival and days out are supplied as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departure timing and southern slant
rubrics_metrics.description: “It will be noticed that all the ships going out in under 80 days ... left the United Kingdom in April, May or June and got a good slant South.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departure month and initial routing (taking a southerly slant early) are presented as critical factors in achieving fast passages; seasonal wind patterns (e.g. hard winds in Channel/N. Atlantic and S.E. trades) are cited to explain why early-summer departures yielded speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily and weekly mileage as performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent reporting of 24-hour runs (e.g., “323 and 330 miles out of her in 48 hours”, lists of daily runs for Samuel Plimsoll, best day’s work 304 miles, best week 2100 miles, averages like 240 miles/day or 284 miles/day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained daily and weekly mileages (and best single-day runs) are used to evaluate a ship’s speed and steadiness; both peak runs and multi-day averages are cited as indicators of performance during specific legs (e.g., equator to S.W. Cape, Cape meridian to Otway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Easting/latitude routing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: References to ‘running the easting down’, keeping the ship in particular latitudes (e.g., “kept her in 39° and 40° S.”, “ran down her easting in 41° S.”) as an element of good passage-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the proper latitude/easting to obtain favorable winds and avoid hazards is shown as a deliberate strategy; examples explain how captains who ran down their easting or chose particular parallels achieved superior averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather impact and delay handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative accounts of being ‘held up by terrific squalls’, ‘had to be brought to under reefed topsails’, ‘was forced down into 47° S. by hard easterly gales’, and statements that squalls or calms could ‘cost her a day’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weather is treated both as a performance limiter and as a factor that explains why otherwise fast ships may be delayed; handling (reefing, waiting for tide/wind shifts) and resulting time costs are illustrated with concrete incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural resilience and seaworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of damage sustained in heavy weather (e.g., ‘came into port with most of her bulwarks gone’, ‘fore and mizen lower topsails blown out of the bolt ropes’, ‘carried away two topmast backstays’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability of a vessel to withstand heavy seas (strength of bulwarks, rigging robustness, topsail resilience) is an implicit quality metric; examples show how damage affects arrival condition and may reflect on ship design or loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design/economic trade-off: carrying capacity vs speed
rubrics_metrics.description: “Competition of steam and reduced freights were making good carrying capacity a necessity for a money-making ship... full-rigged ships of 2000 tons and over were not economical ... the four-mast barque was just as speedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of new ship types (big linerships, four‑mast barques) emphasize the compromise between cargo deadweight and speed; measured averages (e.g., Illawarra’s average under 90 days) and owner decisions (selling Illawarra, buying larger ship) illustrate economic criteria for design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spar plan and canvas (sail area) as performance indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed spar plan (mast heights, yards, topmasts, topgallant masts, royal yards, etc.) and statements like ‘though she did not carry stunsails, she had plenty of canvas.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific spar and yard dimensions are presented as technical attributes that determine sail-carrying capacity, balance and hence speed; the text uses the spar plan to justify statements about the ship’s power and handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparring and ease of steering
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain Pattman: ‘Being perfectly sparred, the ship is easy to steer, and even in the worst weather the smallest boy on board can keep her on her course.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete and well-proportioned spars are linked to good helm balance and ease of steering; this is treated as a practical quality that reduces demands on crew skill in heavy weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steering discipline and accuracy standard
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most strictly adhered to rule on board was that any man or boy found more than half a point off his course was at once sent away from the wheel in disgrace.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrow tolerance for deviation from course (half a point) is reported as a discipline standard that contributes to the ship’s reputation for steady passage‑making; this links human performance/discipline to overall ship performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew composition and apprenticeship training
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain Pattman’s insistence on British crews and his practice of training apprentices (apprentices went to the wheel on their first voyage; he favored ‘sail‑trained’ men over steamship A.B.’s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crew nationality, seamanship background and active apprenticeship (early practical responsibility, progressive duties) are presented as determinants of a ship’s effectiveness and safety; the captain’s testimony recounts improved performance from trained crews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Livestock handling and on‑board procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A ‘new system’ for taking horses on board: walked from railway trucks up gangways on to main deck, down hatchways into stalls; hatch gangways left in position; horses exercised on deck while at sea (every horse getting 24 hours a week on deck). ‘This method proved an unqualified success and saved four days’ time.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedures for embarking, stowing and exercising animals are evaluated by time-savings and animal welfare outcomes; examples include both success (saved four days) and failures (loss of 27 horses and two grooms during bad weather) to illustrate operational risks and best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational crisis procedures for ice/berg encounters
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of encountering dense bergs: ‘called all hands, and after reducing speed to 7 knots sent the hands to their stations... sent the chief mate aloft with a pair of glasses to find a passage out... decided to tack and try and get out the way I had come into the bay.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended emergency seamanship responses include reducing speed, mustering hands to stations, using an aloft lookout with glasses to find a passage, and tacking to escape entrapment; narrative provides a step‑by‑step example of decision-making under ice hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Port/tide entry considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Theophane ‘made no less than three attempts to enter the Heads on the ebb tide, but each time the wind dropped in the rip and she was drifted back and at last was compelled to wait until the next day and come in on the flood.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing arrival and attempting entry with respect to tide and local rip conditions is highlighted as a practical criterion for safe and timely port access; failed attempts show the cost of misjudging tide/wind interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance judged by commercial returns and utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as Loch Torridon clearing £1250 after a voyage (despite expense of grooms and horse food), and Illawarra being sold when considered too small for a contracted cadet/world service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic outcomes (profit on trips, ability to secure lucrative contracts, suitability for new commercial uses) are used as pragmatic measures of a ship’s value beyond published passage times; design and operational choices are assessed for profitability and fit to trade demands.
